⌨️ Terminal Input and Output in TypeScript

In a TypeScript project that runs with Node.js, the terminal is a simple way to interact with your program. You can print messages, ask the user for input, read command-line arguments, and build small tools without needing a browser interface.

What You Need

  • A TypeScript project set up to run with Node.js
  • @types/node installed for Node type support
  • A way to run TypeScript, such as ts-node or a compiled JavaScript output folder

Writing to the Terminal

The fastest way to display output is with console.log(). Use it for normal messages, debugging, or showing results.

Example: Basic Terminal Output

const courseName = "TypeLand";
const lessonCount = 12;

console.log("Welcome to", courseName);
console.log(`This course has ${lessonCount} lessons.`);
console.error("This is an error message.");

Common output methods include console.log(), console.error(), and console.table(). They all write to the terminal, but they are used for slightly different purposes.

Reading Input with readline

To read text that a user types into the terminal, use Node's readline module. It connects your program to standard input and standard output.

Example: Ask the User a Question

import readline from "node:readline";

const rl = readline.createInterface({
  input: process.stdin,
  output: process.stdout,
});

rl.question("What is your name? ", (answer) => {
  console.log(`Hello, ${answer}!`);
  rl.close();
});

This works well for quick scripts, but callback-based code can get harder to read as your program grows.

Using Promises with readline

A cleaner modern approach is to use the promise-based version of readline. That lets you use async and await for a more readable flow.

Example: Async Terminal Input

import readline from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin as input, stdout as output } from "node:process";

async function run(): Promise<void> {
  const rl = readline.createInterface({ input, output });

  const name = await rl.question("What is your name? ");
  const favoriteType = await rl.question("Favorite TypeScript type? ");

  console.log(`Hi ${name}, ${favoriteType} is a solid choice.`);
  rl.close();
}

run().catch((error) => {
  console.error("Program failed:", error);
});

Reading Command-Line Arguments

If you want to pass information into your program without an interactive prompt, use process.argv. This is useful for scripts, tooling, and automation.

Example: Read Arguments from the Terminal

const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const username = args[0] ?? "guest";

console.log(`Running script for ${username}`);

You could run that file like this:

Command

npx ts-node src/terminal-demo.ts ruben

When to Use Each Approach

  • Use console.log() when your program only needs to display information
  • Use readline when you want a user to answer prompts while the program is running
  • Use process.argv when the input should be supplied as part of the command itself

Example: Small Interactive Program

Example: Build a Terminal Greeting Tool

import readline from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin as input, stdout as output } from "node:process";

async function run(): Promise<void> {
  const rl = readline.createInterface({ input, output });

  const username = await rl.question("Username: ");
  const level = await rl.question("Current TypeScript level: ");

  console.log("------------------------------");
  console.log(`User: ${username}`);
  console.log(`Level: ${level}`);
  console.log("Keep practicing your types.");

  rl.close();
}

run().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
});

Tips and Gotchas

💡 Useful Reminders

  • Always close the readline interface with rl.close()
  • Install @types/node if TypeScript does not recognize process or Node modules
  • Use try and catch or .catch() for async programs so failures are visible
  • Prefer command-line arguments when building tools that may be run from scripts or CI pipelines

Quick Start

Commands to Install and Run

npm install typescript ts-node --save-dev
npm install @types/node --save-dev

# Run a file that uses terminal input/output
npx ts-node src/terminal-demo.ts
